facts.text: The common myna is easily recognised by its brown body, black hooded head, bare yellow patch behind the eye and bright yellow bill and legs.
facts.quote: The common myna is readily identified by the brown body, black hooded head and the bare yellow patch behind the eye. The bill and legs are bright yellow.

facts.text: Common mynas are popular cage birds thanks to their singing and ability to mimic speech.
facts.quote: Common mynas are popular as cage birds for their singing and "speaking" abilities.

facts.text: Before settling to sleep in communal roosts, common mynas vocalise together in a chorus known as 'communal noise'.
facts.quote: Before sleeping in communal roosts, common mynas vocalise in unison, which is known as "communal noise".

facts.text: Common mynas are believed to mate for life, and birds are usually seen in pairs.
facts.quote: Common mynas are believed to pair for life.

facts.text: Mynas build nests from twigs, roots, tow and rubbish, and have even used tissue paper, tin foil and sloughed-off snake skin.
facts.quote: Nesting material used by common mynas includes twigs, roots, tow and rubbish. Common mynas have been known to use tissue paper, tin foil and sloughed off snake-skin.

facts.text: The common myna eats everything from grasshoppers and earthworms to fruit, nectar, roadkill and discarded human food.
facts.quote: It feeds on insects, grubs, earthworms, arachnids, crustaceans, reptiles, small mammals, seeds, grain, fruits, flower nectar and petals, and discarded waste from human habitation.

facts.text: The genus name Acridotheres means 'grasshopper hunter', earned from the myna's habit of foraging for grasshoppers on the ground.
facts.quote: It forages on the ground among grass for insects, and especially for grasshoppers, from which it gets the generic name Acridotheres, "grasshopper hunter".

facts.text: In Canberra, just 110 mynas released between 1968 and 1971 gave rise to an average density of 15 birds per square kilometer by 1991.
facts.quote: in Canberra, for instance, 110 common mynas were released between 1968 and 1971. By 1991, common myna population density in Canberra averaged 15 birds per square kilometer.
